Good morning. I call to order the High Level Forum on the Programme of Action on a Culture of Peace. This meeting is held in accordance with resolution 80/294 of July 24, 2026, under the theme Women's Leadership to Promote a Culture of Peace. As mentioned in my letters dated August 6 and 25, and September 1st, 2026, this meeting will consist of an opening segment and a plenary segment. I will now make a statement as the president of the General Assembly. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, 80 years ago, our United Nations was created with the express purpose of saving succeeding generation from the scourge of war. Yet our founding mothers and fathers had the wisdom, foresight, and especially experience to know that peace is more than the absence of war. Therefore, they thought to build an institution not focused narrowly on peace and security, but upon the mutually reinforcing pillars of human rights, sustainable development, and peace and security. So while today some call for the United Nations to go back to basics, we should remember that the pursuit of a just, sustainable and lasting peace is indeed one of our basics. It is embedded in the very foundation of this organization and it lies at the heart of the culture of peace. The conviction that lasting peace requires replacing violence with dialogue, division with mutual understanding and cooperation and inclusion with participation. Since the adoption of the Declaration and Programme of Action on a Culture of Peace in 1999, at the initiative of Bangladesh, this Assembly has continued to advance that vision of a more peaceful, just and inclusive world. Central to this effort is the full, equal, meaningful and safe participation of women in peace processes. That is why the theme of this year's high-level forum, women's leadership to promote a culture of peace, could not be more important and timely. Including women at every stage of peace process is not just nice to have. It's not doing a favor to women. It is not even simply a matter of fairness. It is fundamentally a question of whether peace succeeds It's in the interest of all of us, of every society. As research has shown that when women participate meaningfully in peace processes, the probability of an agreement lasting at least two years increases by 20%. And the probability of conflict returning is reduced by 37%. That is because women bring the experiences, knowledge, and priorities of half of the world's population to the negotiation table. the society approach. They broaden negotiations beyond the conduct of war and armed actors to the communities and people that they are affected by it. And they raise issues that create the conditions for peace to firmly take root, from conflict-related sexual violence and access to justice, to economic opportunity and political participation at all levels. Or as a woman who I met at the front lines told me, If women are safe, everyone is safe. Because when more voices and perspectives are included when shaping peace, the outcome will better reflect the realities of the people who will benefit from it, and peace will be more likely to endure. History has given us powerful examples of women's role in peace. In Colombia, women-led advocacy helped ensure that the landmark 2016 agreement between the government and the Revolutionary Armed Forces addressed critical issues such as victims' rights, land access, and conflict-related sexual violence. And in Liberia, Christian and Muslim women came together across religious and social divides to pray, organize, and demonstrate for peace. Through the Women of Liberia Mass Action for Peace, they pushed political leaders and armed actors towards peace by bringing their demands directly to the negotiation process in Accra. I'm therefore especially honored that today we are joined by Ms. Leymah Gbowee, Nobel Peace Prize laureate, and one of the pioneer leaders of that movement to learn from your experience. Ms. Gbowee's unwavering bravery and tenacity to mobilize communities and demand accountability is not simply an inspiration to admire from afar. It is a rallying call to give women the power to shape peace in every conflict. This assembly has affirmed that principle time and again. The 2025 review of the United Nations peacebuilding architecture recognized that the full, equal, meaningful, and safe participation of women at all decision-making levels in conflict resolution is key to achieving durable solutions and long-term stability. The architecture recognizes the role of women in prevention and resolution of conflicts, in peacebuilding and in building critical foundations for promoting a culture of peace. Ladies and gentlemen, our commitments are clear. The history speaks for itself and the data is unequivocal. Yet there remains a profound gap between what we know and what we are doing. At a time when the number of armed conflicts is at a record high, too many negotiation tables still exclude women that hold the keys to unlocking peace. Frankly speaking, you only have to look at the most recent photos or media coverage of the last peace negotiations, where there are hardly any women in the room. And also frankly speaking, if you look at our regular government coalitions these days, Often there is also not a single woman present. And even in the teams programming the next AI algorithm, where we know that AI will play a crucial role in the conflicts of the future, still they are not designed with the voices of women. So it doesn't only start at the end, at the peace negotiation table. It starts here today in our own meetings, in our own CEO setups, in our own culture. As said, this is not only a question of injustice. It is a missed opportunity for sustained peace to leave women out of the room. If we are serious about fulfilling the promise made 80 years ago to have succeeding generation from the scourge of war, then our commitments must be matched by our actions. A culture of peace is not an abstract aspiration. It is a choice every one of us makes every day throughout societies. And it is our collective responsibility to build societies where we uphold the principles of the UN Charter and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. where we safeguard justice and dignity for all, and where we ensure that women are not observers of peace, but are actively building it. Because if women are safe, everyone is safe. I thank you and I give the floor to Ms. Elizabeth Speier, Assistant Secretary General for Peacebuilding and Peace Support. Please.

Thank you very much, Madam President, Madam Chair, Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, ladies and gentlemen. I want to thank you all for this very important exchange that you will be having today. Today, violent conflict is increasing in both number and complexity. Political polarization is deepening, humanitarian crises are multiplying, and we're witnessing growing pushback against gender equality, women's leadership, and civic space. Yet evidence from across regions shows that peace is more durable and sustainable when women participate meaningfully in shaping it. This is a cornerstone of the Women, Peace and Security agenda and the sustaining peace resolutions. Women's leadership is central to building a culture of peace. Women around the world already demonstrate what this leadership can look like. They mediate disputes when they escalate. strengthen social cohesion in divided societies, advocate for justice, and help communities recover from conflict. Women-led organizations also broaden the peacebuilding agenda by bringing attention to issues that are often overlooked, including community security, mental health and psychosocial support, and gender-based violence. The message is that women are not just beneficiaries of peacebuilding, they are critical architects of peace. We see this clearly, for example, in our efforts to promote women's leadership in security and justice institutions. In Somalia, women lawyers are occupying higher positions in the judiciary, opening pathways to leadership while making justice more accessible to women and girls. In Syria and Nepal, women now sit on national transitional justice bodies, bringing a broader range of experience. into decisions about justice and recovery. In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, women are helping shape the rules themselves. Evidence that they have presented on barriers facing women in the security sector is now informing the country's forthcoming national security policy. These experiences show that women's leadership is not only changing who is represented in institutions, it's also changing how justice and security are understood and delivered. I'm pleased that the United Nations will soon launch the UN portal on women in justice and security, bringing together global data and good practices on women's participation and leadership across justice and security institutions. I thank member states that have already contributed to this effort, and I would encourage others to share data and good practices as well, and to nominate women leaders to help review the portal's findings and inform further progress. So how do we ensure that more women and women-led organizations are able to exercise this leadership for a culture of peace? First, we must protect and further expand civic space in many constrained contexts. Women peacebuilders and civil society organizations must be able to participate freely, safely, and meaningfully in all political and peace processes. The Secretary General's 2025 report on women, peace and security warns that shrinking civic space and growing attacks on women activists are undermining hard won gains. A culture of peace cannot flourish where voices are silenced. It requires open civic space, inclusive dialogue, civilian oversight and control, civilian oversight and control of security and justice institutions. and sectors, and meaningful participation by those working every day to sustain peace in their communities. One lesson emerges consistently across contexts. Peacebuilding is strongest when it is participatory, locally led, and broadly inclusive. Second, women's leadership must influence decisions that shape political transitions, peace processes, prevention, recovery, and justice and security policies. at all levels, including national and global policy forums. That is why we're planning to convene next year the first global conference on women leaders in justice and security to address gaps, promote international cooperation, and ensure that their perspectives are reflected in UN policymaking. The Peacebuilding Commission also demonstrates the value of women peacebuilders engaging directly and systematically with Member States and the United Nations, strengthening peacebuilding policy and practice across the UN system. The annual Civil Society UN Peacebuilders Dialogue offers another valuable space. This year's dialogue will focus on promoting civic space at a time of rising authoritarianism. Last year, more than 187 civil society organizations and over 40 UN entities and member state representatives participated, with women peacebuilders and leaders making up 57% of participants. We expect women to again make up the majority of participants this year. Third, we must invest more and more directly in women's peacebuilding organizations and their work. Despite global commitments, women-led organizations, including those preventing violence, facilitating dialogue, and supporting recovery, remain too often at the margins of peacebuilding financing and decision-making. That is why the Secretary-General's Peacebuilding Fund places a strong emphasis on gender-responsive peacebuilding and women's meaningful participation and leadership, with 30% of its annual investment directed towards these objectives, a target that the Peacebuilding Fund has consistently surpassed since 2018. Excellencies, let me close with one further reflection. Building a culture of peace means building a global constituency for peace. Much of the strength of that constituency that we need to build will depend on how we support, empower and mentor the next generation of women leaders. This requires looking at the women, peace and security and youth peace and security agendas together. Preliminary information from a forthcoming study on youth contributions to peace, mandated by the Pact for the Future, points to the double exclusion experienced by many young women, whose realities and concerns are not fully addressed by either agenda on its own. We must take up this challenge. Let us pursue our commitments to women's leadership and youth leadership in tandem, not in parallel, so that young women are recognized and supported as leaders for peace today, not just tomorrow. Our task is clear to ensure that women's leadership at all levels is recognized, protected, resourced, and shaping the decisions of our collective future. Please allow me to finish by thanking the President of the General Assembly for her outstanding leadership and guidance and wishing her every success in her next chapter. Thank you.

Thank you, and also thank you for your personal remarks. I thank this Assistant Secretary General for Peacebuilding and Peace Support. I now give the floor to His Excellency Anwarul Chowdhury, former Under-Secretary General and High Representative of the United Nations and founder of the Global Movement for the Culture of Peace.

Thank you, thank you, Madam President. I would like to begin by thanking you for a very powerful and meaningful statement, opening statement. We appreciate that. And I have the special pleasure in welcoming Laima, Laima Bojaitiene, because she was on previous occasion as the keynote speaker in the High Level Forum on the Culture of Peace. So I'm very happy she joined us this time again. And I have also a great pleasure in welcoming the permanent representative, the new permanent representative of Bangladesh. She is here and I am very happy that Bangladesh mission is now headed by a woman leader. And that's a wonderful opportunity for me to meet her for the first time in this meeting. Madam President, in 11 days from today, on 13 September, the United Nations will observe the 27th anniversary of the General Assembly's unanimous adoption of the Declaration and Programme of Action on a Culture of Peace. This high-level forum convened by you, Madam President, provides the most appropriate setting for the celebration of this remarkable pathway to the global culture of peace as articulated by its apex body. The theme of this forum, rightfully, is women's leadership to promote the culture of peace. If I may add here that you yourself, Madam President, is a true embodiment of the core focus of this theme in your leadership of the United Nations General Assembly as one of its five women presidents among the 80 individuals gracing this position since the birth of this organization. Mandated by the UN General Assembly, UN resolutions, the successive presidents of the General Assembly have been convening the annual high-level forums, attracting the attention of member states and civil society since 2012, when your predecessor, PGA 66, Ambassador Al-Nasser, took the initiative to convene the first forum. The forum has the distinction of being the only UN gathering which was addressed by the largest number of Nobel Peace Laureates. all women, and I again recognize Lima's presence here, six time out of 11 forums. Also, the forums panelists were always gender balanced on most occasions with more women participating. As the United Nations Under Secretary General and High Representative for the most vulnerable countries, And as the permanent representative of Bangladesh, my work has taken me to the farthest corners of the world. And I have seen time and again the centrality of women's equality and the culture of peace in our lives. This realization has now become more pertinent in the midst of the ever-increasing militarism, militarization and weaponization that is destroying both our planet and our people. As we all know, the Charter of the United Nations, when signed in 1945, was the first international agreement to affirm the principle of equality between women and men. The Programme of Action on Culture of Peace accords a place of prominence to equality between women and men, fourth among its eight action areas. Women represent more than half of the global population, yet they continue to be underrepresented in leadership positions in every region of the world. Unfortunately, in recent years, women's rights are under threat from a backlash of conservatism and fundamentalism around the world. Let me assert again that patriarchy and misogyny are the dual scourges pulling humanity back from our aspiration for a better world to live in freedom, equality, and justice. On 8th of March, 2000, as the president of the UN Security Council, I could initiate and mobilize the council to recognize unanimously in a statement that, and I quote, peace is inextricably linked with equality between women and men," end of quote, and affirmed the value of full and equal participation of women at all decision-making levels. That is when the seed for the UN Security Council Resolution 1325 was sown. It was finally adopted on the 31st of October of the same year. We should never forget that when women, more than half of the world's eight billion plus people, are marginalized, there is no chance for our world to get sustainable peace in the real sense. It is my strong belief that unless women are engaged in advancing the culture of peace at equal levels at all times with men, sustainable peace would continue to elude us. In various parts of the world, women have shown great capacity as peace builders. At the grassroots and community levels, women have organized to resist militarization, to create space for dialogue and moderation, and to weave together the shattered fabric of society. As I reiterate time and again, women bring a new breadth, quality, and balance of vision to a common effort of moving away from the cult of war towards the culture of peace. Women's equality makes our planet safe and secure. The slogan of global campaign on women, peace and security, which we launched in London in June 2014 reiterates, and I quote, "If we are serious about peace, we must take women seriously." End of quote. Let me end by emphasizing that feminism is not intended to pit women against men or men against women. Feminism is about smart policy, which is inclusive, uses all potential, and leaves no one behind. I am proud to be a feminist. All of us need to be. That is how we make our planet a better place to live for all. We should always remember that without peace, development is impossible. And without development, peace is not achievable. But without women, neither peace nor development is conceivable. I continue to emphasize that the culture of peace is not a quick fix. It is a movement, not a revolution. And women always bolster that movement immensely. Let me conclude by underscoring here an unacceptable reality. In its 81 years of existence, The United Nations has not yet elected a woman Secretary-General. Eight decades plus, nine men, not one woman. What an embarrassment. What a shame. How can an institution that speaks of equality at every podium continues to model inequality at its pinnacle? The credibility of the UN's advocacy depends on its own reflection in the mirror. I thank you for your kind attention.

I'm glad to be sharing this space again with you, Ambassador Chaudhry, and to other colleagues in the room. 12 years ago, I sat in this very room to speak on the culture of peace. And the climate conversation had just ended in Peru, laying the groundworks for the Paris Agreement a year later. That same year, we were preparing to celebrate the 15th anniversary of the UN Security Council Resolution 1325 as women peacebuilders. In those moments as we prepared, we hoped our world would finally not only recognize our unique skills and potentials in conflict resolution and building peace in our communities, but strategically engage us as partners and thought leaders in the quest for peace in our world. Fortunately or unfortunately, that will not be the case and the struggle continues. I am one of the thousands of women in Liberia who worked for years to end the Liberian civil war. In those years, we worked at the local level in different ways to end the war. However, I wish I could say our processes were connected. At the beginning, we were disconnected and it perpetuated a lot of divisions that separated our country and us as women. Many of us recognize the futility of working separately. So the question we ask ourselves, how can we extinguish the fire of war with drops of water? And how can we extinguish the fire of war with a divisive mentality? We came together, formed the Women of Liberia Mass Action for Peace, and Madam President spoke about it earlier on, bringing together Christian and Muslim women. This marriage was far from easy. There was no honeymoon. We got married and we had to start working. Our group included women from different income levels, rural and urban areas, ethnicity and faith. In those early days, we spent many days negotiating amongst ourselves in order to resolve the conflicts that came up. Contrary to popular belief that grassroots women peace efforts lack planning, coordination and strategy, we as Liberian women, like many other women across the world, were intentional. We planned every day for hours. We deliberately sought out actors who would further our cause and build strategic alliances in the course of our work. In that struggle, we inadvertently carry out the first mandate of Article One in the Declaration of the Culture of Peace. And this article says, education through education, dialogue and cooperation, we fostered an environment of conducive to peace. It is not easy as peace building is never easy. But in doing so, we expanded our initial goal of ending the Liberian civil war. We committed to building a culture of peace in a nation that had been devastated by war. One million of our compatriots were internally displaced, 500,000 were refugees. At that time, our population was about 3 million, and we have an estimate 250,000 people who lost their lives. So just to give you a picture that we were able to kill at least almost 10% of our population in 14 years of civil war. When negotiations failed in 1996 and '99, the women of Liberia were able to contribute to lasting peace. I can emphatically say, 23 years without the resurgence of violence last August made it 23 years in Liberia is largely due to the community, specifically the women's active involvement, not just in 2003, a must state, but from 2003, we have consistently continued to engage, ensuring that peace and the peace process remains on course. If peace was never handed to the Liberian women, We labored, we persevere, and recreated a culture of respect and constructive engagement. This year, our world is in a maze of conflict and global issues. The geopolitical instability marred by competition and fragmentation, trade tensions and supply chains disruption, climate and environmental crisis, AI is source of opportunities and concern. False information and information manipulation are deepening political and social divisions and undermining public trust in governments and democratic processes. And in all of this, women continue to suffer. As we gather to consider the programs of action on the culture of peace, we must consider these three factors, one, A culture of peace therefore requires more than absence of conflict. It requires inclusion, justice, dignity, dialogue, and in the world that we live in today, dialogue is far from everything that we do. It's either you agree with me, or if you disagree, we can't have a conversation. And the willingness to build relationship across political divide. religious, ethnic, and social divides. In a world of increasing political intolerance, my question to you all, Your Excellency, is this possible to achieve? The second part, a culture of peace becomes possible when women are not simply invited to participate, but are recognized as leaders, decision makers, and builders of a more just and inclusive society. For too long, women's involvement in these processes has been decorative. Sometimes I refuse invitations to come to the UN, just saying what Ambassador Chardley said, 80 years of male dominance, now is the time for women's leadership at the UN. We continue to see resistance or welfare amnesia in women's full and effective participation in building a culture of peace and peacebuilding work. Women across the world have been tested, have been proven worthy of building peace at all levels. We don't need to build a strong case on the behalf of women anymore. Unlike many global peace processes, women have the track record. It is our role now as leaders in this room to help elevate women's peacebuilding work and review the difference in how national and global peace is negotiated. Women peacebuilding is not centered solely on deconstructing war, it is about building a culture of peace. Today's affirmation is more importantly a challenge. The United Nations, as we all sit here, is as strong as its member state. And all of the member state in this room is weak without its people. And by saying people, I mean all genders. When we have elections in our countries, it's not just the men that vote, the women vote also. So it is important that men as well as women play a critical role in creating the culture of peace. The third part is resources. Many speakers talked about it. The assistant secretary general talked about resources. We use billions to make war. We cannot use peanuts to build peace. Now is the time if we're serious about building a culture of peace and involving women, we must give them the necessary resources. But let me just emphatically state here, that I'm really very proud of women across the world, despite the shrinking spaces, the shrinking resources, despite the political pushback that we've received. Women are no longer waiting because we recognize that with or without donors funding, we become the ones who bear the greatest brunt in every crisis. So they continue, we continue to work to keep our communities and our societies stable. So I think we must continue to applaud the efforts of women whilst the world continue to watch and wait, women continue to do amazing work in their different countries. I sincerely believe that the ultimate goal of all of our activities globally is to create a culture of peace that promotes respect of rights of others in a world where we all live in harmony. This goal is achievable. However, it will take hard work, thinking outside of the box, political will, and sincerity. I will end with this, giving each and every one of us in this room a homework. And the homework is as you go home today, look at your children, look at your community, look at your nation, think about the culture of peace and ask yourself, can we continue to do peace building without the hands of everyone? Can we continue to operate our world leaving women behind if we're serious about building a culture of peace for our children and the next generation? We must sit and answer these questions sincerely. Thank you, Madam President.

Women's voices must be heard, their experiences must be valued, and their leadership must be recognized if societies are to build and sustain a culture of peace. I thank the distinguished representative of Bangladesh and a warm welcome, Madam Ambassador, to the United Nations in New York. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Turkmenistan on behalf of the Group of Friends of Neutrality for Peace, Security and Sustainable Development.

Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I have the honour to deliver this statement on behalf of the Group.

Of Friends of Neutrality for Peace, security and sustainable development.

At the outset, the group expresses its appreciation to the President of the General Assembly for convening this high-level forum and welcomes its timely focus on women's leadership to promote a culture of peace. The group welcomes the recent adoption of GA resolution 18/294, follow-up to the Declaration and Programme of Action on a Culture of Peace. At a time of growing geopolitical tensions, conflicts mistrust and polarization its message is particularly relevant peace must not be understood simply as the interval between phases of conflict it must be actively built and sustained through dialogue Mutual respect inclusion Justice and cooperation for the group of friends the culture of peace and the principles of neutrality are closely interconnected this connection has been further reinforces by the recent General Assembly resolution 262, the role and importance of a policy of neutrality in maintaining and strengthening international peace, security and sustainable development. The Group therefore welcomes the strong emphasis in resolution 80/294 on gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls. and on advancing women's full, equal and meaningful participation in conflict prevention, peacebuilding and activities promoting a culture of peace. Second, greater support should be provided to women mediators, peacebuilders and women-led organizations, including through capacity building and professional networks. Following the 2025 parliamentary elections, women now hold one third of the seats in parliament, while at the local level their representation has approached 40%. This progress reflects not only greater equality of opportunity, but also contributes to more inclusive, effective and resilient institutions. The Kyrgyz Republic firmly believes that Investing in women's leadership is an investment in the resilience of society. Creating greater opportunities for women to participate fully in public and political life helps foster a culture of dialogue, trust, and nonviolence. In this context, women's leadership should be viewed not only as a matter of equal rights and opportunities, but also as a strategic imperative for--.
I thank the representative of Kyrgyzstan. I now give the floor to the representative of Brazil.

Thank you, Mr. Chair. A culture of peace and human rights are intrinsically linked and mutually reinforcing. Sustainable peace requires justice, development, and the full realization of civil, political, economic, social, and cultural rights. It also demands non-discrimination and the full participation of women.

Because peace is shaped by and with women.

Brazil has stood firmly by this perspective since the very beginning of this organization. In 1945, Brazilian Bertha Lutz, one of the very few women at the San Francisco Conference, firstly advocated for the inclusion of a reference to women alongside men in the preamble of the charter, making gender equality a constitutive mandate for the UN. Bertha Lutz's lesson and example remain vivid in Brazil's actions and aspirations. Brazil supports women participating fully, equally, meaningfully, and safely in peace and security, as well as on all aspects of public life. That includes their role as community leaders, mediators, human rights defenders, and peacekeepers. It means bringing a necessary gender perspective into mandates, planning and engagement with local communities. It also includes their full participation at the table where decisions are being made. Brazil has sought to translate this principle into action. We participate in the Ibero-American Network of Women Mediators and the Regional Network of Women Mediators of the Southern Cone. We also joined the Secretary-General's Common Pledge for women's full, equal and meaningful participation in peace processes from the moment of its launch. Moreover, more than 300 Brazilian women have served as peacekeepers in different missions. Brazil also values the important role of the Peacebuilding Commission in this regard. It can give greater visibility to women mediators, support locally owned initiatives, and strengthen coherence among international actors. In this sense, it is essential that women's participation be mainstreamed across prevention, mediation, peacebuilding, and peacekeeping. It should also be present at every level from the UN headquarters to the local communities. This spirit is also reflected in Brazil's and Mexico's support for Michelle Bachelet's candidacy for the position of United Nations Secretary General. Her candidacy represents an opportunity to elect the first woman Secretary General, as well as to have a representative from Latin America at the helm of the organization.

I thank you.
I thank Brazil, and I give the floor to the representative of Nepal.

Mr. President, Nepal welcomes the convening of this important annual high-level forum. It's a time when global peace and multilateralism are under unprecedented strains. Strengthening a culture of peace is an urgent imperative and our shared responsibility. This requires justice, equality, inclusion, respect for human rights, and meaningful participation of women in decisions that shape our governance and societies. This year's theme, focusing on women's leadership, resonates deeply with Nepal's national priorities and lived experience. Nepal therefore supports the WPS agenda and remains committed to advancing women's full, equal, meaningful and safe participation at all levels of peace and political processes. We are equally committed to the full and effective implementation of the Programme of Action on a Culture of Peace. Our homegrown and nationally led peace process demonstrates the indispensable role of women in mediation, reconciliation, social mobilization and peacebuilding. Our constitution guarantees equality, social justice, proportional inclusion, and mandates at least 33% representation of women in the federal parliament and provincial assemblies, and 40% in local bodies. These commitments are reinforced by the national gender equality policy, gender responsive budgeting now exceeding 44%, and laws addressing gender-based violence and access to justice. On a positive note, women in Nepal represent over 34% in federal House of Representatives, 40% of elected position in local bodies, about 30% of the civil service, about 40% of school teachers, and more than 10% of security forces. Nearly three quarters of deputy mayors and vice chairpersons are women, many leading local judicial committees that bring justice, mediation, and protection closer to communities. Nepal also take pride in being among the top contributors of female peacekeepers who build trust, engage with communities, and protect civilians. Its persistent challenges, including inequalities, underrepresentation, and lack of access to resources are stuck. Mr. President, let me highlight few key points. First, institutionalize women's leadership across the entire peace continuum as their role is vital to conflict prevention, mediation, peace building, and reconstruction, and ensure tangible progress on the 2030 agenda, particularly SDG five. Nepal stands fast to working with the broader UN membership and all partners to anchor women leadership at the heart of our collective endeavors.

Thank you.
I thank the representative of Nepal. I now give the floor to the representative of Qatar.

Mr. President, at the outset, I would like to thank you for convening this high-level forum on the program of action on a culture of peace under the theme women's leadership to promote culture of peace. I also thank the distinguished panelists for their valuable contributions. The State of Qatar reiterates its full support for the Declaration and Programme of Action on a Culture of Peace and its effective implementation. More than 25 years after its adoption, this message remains as important as ever. A culture of peace is not simply the absence of conflict. It requires respect for international law and human rights, justice and equality, tolerance and solidarity, and a commitment to dialogue and the peaceful settlement of disputes. Against the backdrop of today's global challenges, these principles are more important than ever. Let me convey three brief points. First, there can be no sustainable culture of peace without the full, equal, and meaningful participation of women. Women must not only be protected from the consequences of conflict, they must be leaders in preventing conflict, building peace, and shaping the decisions that affect their societies. This is a priority for the state of Qatar. We remain firmly committed to the Women, Peace and Security agenda and to creating greater opportunities for women to participate in dialogue, mediation and decision-making. Qatar has joined the Secretary-General's Common Pledge for women's full, equal and meaningful participation in peace processes and is an active member of the Arab Women Mediators Network. Through the Qatar Fund for Development's Women in Conflict Zones Initiative, Qatar also supports women and girls affected by conflict, promoting their role as agents of change and peacemakers in the communities. Second, building a culture of peace requires us to invest in prevention and address the root causes of conflict. For Qatar, this means a continued commitment to mediation, dialogue, and preventive diplomacy, fundamental pillars of our foreign policy. It also means investing in education. Quality and inclusive education, particularly for women and girls and children affected by conflict, is one of the most powerful tools we have to promote tolerance, opportunity, economic empowerment, and peaceful societies. Third, a culture of peace requires effective multilateralism founded on international law and with a strong United Nations at its core. At a time when the multilateral system is under enormous pressure, we need United Nations capable of responding effectively to today's challenges. It is in this spirit that the State of Qatar fully supports the UNAD initiative and efforts to make our organization more effective, accountable, and responsive. Mr. President, the challenge before us is to turn our shared commitment to a culture of peace into a lived reality for all. The State of Qatar will continue its efforts to translate this commitment into concrete action. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Qatar. I now give the floor to the representative of Azerbaijan.

Mr. President, the full text of the statement will be circulated in writing. We would like to express our gratitude for convening the high-level forum commemorating the adoption of the declaration and program of action on the culture of peace. Azerbaijan firmly believes that progress towards the full development of a culture of peace can be achieved through values, attitudes, modes of behavior, and ways of life conducive to the promotion of peace among individuals, groups, and nations. Our society is inherently multicultural and multi-confessional with a history of peaceful coexistence that has endured for centuries. The government remains committed to taking consistent measures to promote tolerance and mutual understanding both nationally and internationally. As part of these efforts, Azerbaijan organizes the Forum on Intercultural Dialogue biennially, and this year, the seventh World Forum will be held under the theme Dialogue for a Shared Future: Building Bridges in a Fractured World from 27 to 29 October 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. Mr. President, the program of action particularly emphasizes the role of women and the importance of their great involvement in the prevention and resolution of conflicts, as well as in activities promoting a culture of peace in post-conflict situations. Despite the end of the decades-long conflict and the progress achieved in advancing the peace agenda in our region, Azerbaijan continues to face the pressing issue of missing persons. The fate and whereabouts of more than 4,000 Azerbaijanis including 287 women, remain unknown. Clarifying the fate of missing persons and advancing related international efforts on matters of particular significance. Azerbaijan is undertaking large-scale rehabilitation and reconstruction efforts in the post-conflict period to enable internally displaced persons to exercise their right to return safely, voluntarily, and with dignity to their places of origin. Through the Greater Return Program, specific measures have been introduced to support the empowerment of women and girls and to facilitate their meaningful participation in the recovery process. However, the safe, voluntary, and dignified return of the population is seriously hindered by the extensive contamination of the conflict-affected territories with landmines and other explosive remnants of war. Azerbaijan carrying out systematic mine action measures, including paying particular attention to the agenda dimension. Mr. President, in conclusion, I would like to reiterate Azerbaijan's strong commitment to taking effective measures at all levels to promote the values of a culture of peace in accordance with the program of action and other relevant international frameworks, including through the promotion of mutual understanding, dialogue, and cooperation.

Thank you.
I thank the representative of Azerbaijan. I now give the floor to the representative of Saudi Arabia.

Mr. President, Excellencies, at the outset, I would like to thank the President of the General Assembly for holding this high-level forum and for her efforts to strengthen the culture of peace and to highlight the role of women in building peace. The Kingdom believes that the culture of peace is not just the absence of conflict. We are strengthening the values of dialogue, tolerance, and strengthening the full participation of women in building safe and prosperous societies and addressing challenges given the many conflicts and wars around the world. We need to enable women so that they can participate fully as this is a main pillar to achieve sustainable development and strengthen peace and security. Based on our 2030 vision, we took a number of steps to strengthen the participation of women in a number of areas and to expand her participation in decision-making processes and to also enable women to participate effectively at the political, social, and humanitarian levels. We also saw progress in the participation of Saudi women in diplomacy and in holding leadership positions and their participation in Saudi missions and in different international organizations. when planning for humanitarian and relief programs in order to reflect women's participation in strengthening international dialogue. Ladies and gentlemen, we pay special attention to women's role in conflict prevention and settlement and in humanitarian efforts. We reaffirm the important role of women in mediation and prevention and in building societies that are more resilient. My country is also making relevant efforts to advance the women peace and security agenda because we believe that the participation of women could strengthen and sustain peace. The Kingdom also strengthens the culture of peace at the national level through the efforts of our national center to build bridges, to guarantee social cohesion, and through national initiatives to enable young people and to spread the values of tolerance and strengthen dialogue between people and civilizations. In conclusion, we reaffirm that women are an essential partner in building peace and strengthening stability and sustainable development.

I thank you.
I thank the representative of Saudi Arabia. I now give the floor to the representative of Egypt.

Thank you so much, Mr. President, Excellencies, esteemed delegates. Egypt is pleased to participate in this high-level forum on the program of action on a culture of peace, which provides an important opportunity to reaffirm our collective commitment to advancing a culture of peace at a time when conflicts, polarization, intolerance, and growing humanitarian crises continue to affect millions around the world. We particularly welcome this year's focus on women's leadership to promote a culture of peace. Women are not merely beneficiaries of peace. They are indispensable partners in building, sustaining, and protecting it. Their full, equal, and meaningful participation strengthens societies, contributes to conflict prevention and resolution, and enhances the prospects for sustainable and lasting peace. Egypt remains committed to advancing women's empowerment and participation across political, economic, and social life, and to strengthening their contribution to peace building and sustainable development, we also emphasize the importance of investing in education, economic opportunities, and capacity building for women and girls. Egypt has consistently supported the Women, Peace and Security agenda and the implementation of Security Council Resolution 1325. We underscore that women's participation must extend throughout the peace continuum, from prevention and mediation to peacebuilding, reconstruction and development. And that particular attention must be paid to women living under conflict and occupation. Excellencies, more than a quarter of a century after the adoption of the Declaration and Programme of Action on a Culture of Peace, their principles remain as relevant as ever. A genuine culture of peace requires respect for the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations and the international law, including respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states and the peaceful settlement of disputes, and non-interference in international affairs, and respect for the right of people to self-determination. Egypt believes that promoting a culture of peace cannot be separated from addressing the root causes of conflict and instability poverty, inequality, occupation, discrimination, exclusion and the denial of fundamental rights create conditions in which violence and instability can flourish. Our efforts must therefore place prevention and sustainable development at their core while ensuring that all people are able to live in dignity, security and freedom. In the end, Egypt will continue to work with all partners to advance a culture of peace grounded in the Charter, respect for international law and the equal dignity for all people. Thank you.
I thank the representative of Egypt. I give the floor to the representative of Armenia.

Mr. President, Excellencies, dialogue, tolerance and respect for diversity are indispensable for safeguarding human dignity and building peaceful and inclusive societies. Yet amid deepening polarization and intolerance, the foundation of peaceful coexistence are increasingly under strain, with women often disproportionately affected by conflict and violence. Against this backdrop, the declaration and program of action on culture of peace together with relevant GA resolutions continue to provide an important framework for concerted international action. We remain firmly committed to promoting a culture of peaceful prevention at the core of our approach. At the UN, including through resolutions of the General Assembly and the Human Rights Council, Armenia has consistently contributed to strengthening international efforts to prevent discrimination and violence. Education is equally integral to building peaceful societies, strengthening resilience against prejudice and discrimination while nurturing respect for diversity. In this spirit, Armenia initiated the GA resolution Education for Peace, adopted by consensus this June, recognizing the wider role of education in promoting tolerance, mutual understanding, and a culture of peace. Mr. President, Armenia particularly welcomes the forum's focus on women's leadership and recognizing that women's full, meaningful participation across peace and security is essential to advancing conflict prevention and achieving sustainable and lasting peace. This commitment is reflected in Armenia's implementation of the WPS agenda as an integral part of our broader commitment to democratic governance, human rights, and sustainable peace. Our third national action plan on WPS entitled Investing in Global Efforts for Peace seeks to advance women's participation and leadership in conflict prevention and peace building while safeguarding the protection of the rights of women and vulnerable populations affected by conflict. Women's political participation also remains an important priority for Armenia, including through their representation in elected institutions, with women constituting over 35% of the newly elected National Assembly. Mr. President, Armenia stands ready to work with all partners to advance tolerance and non-discrimination, promote women's full, equal, and meaningful participation in peace processes, and foster a culture of peace in accordance with the UN Charter and the Declaration and Programme of Action on a Culture of Peace. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Armenia. I give the floor to the representative of Tunisia.

Thank you, Mr. President, Excellencies. We cannot talk about a culture of peace without addressing the threats that undermine peace, notably terrorism and violent extremism. These efforts cannot be successful without the full participation and leadership of women. Experiences have shown that we cannot just look at women as victims. Women and girls bear the brunt of the dangerous repercussions of terrorism and violent extremism, including sexual violence, trafficking in persons, displacement, and the violation of basic rights. At the same time, women play an important role in prevention, early warning, and confronting the rhetoric of extremism and strengthening the resilience of communities. Tunisia has sought to translate this conviction into tangible measures by adopting a national action plan for the implementation of Security Council Resolution 1325 on women, peace and security. And within our priorities, we included prevention from extremism and terrorism and strengthening the role of women in building peace. Mr. President, participation of women is a main pillar in preventing terrorism and violent extremism. This role starts from family where women equally alongside fathers contribute to raising their children on the values of tolerance and moderation and in protecting children from hate speech and extreme ideas. Women also play an important role in identifying indicators of extremism, we believe in the importance of strengthening the participation of women in all stages to combat terrorism from prevention, awareness, decision-making, rehabilitation and reintegration. The more present women are in society and decision-making processes, communities can then protect their children from extremism and communities are stronger in confronting terrorism. The fight against terrorism starts before carrying guns and the loss of lives. It starts with fighting terrorism, starts with education, awareness and prevention and strengthening the participation of women in the decision making process. empowering women in this fight is empowering families, protecting generations, and strengthening policies and decisions, and supporting the security and stability of society.

I thank you.
I thank the representative of Tunisia. I now give the floor to the representative of Costa Rica.

Mr. President, Costa Rica welcomes the convening of this forum and joins the call to strengthen women's leadership as a cornerstone of a genuine and sustainable culture of peace. The figures speak for themselves. Between 2022 and 2023, only 0.4% of bilateral aid to conflict-affected contexts, equivalent to $186 million annually, reached women-led organizations, well below the 1% minimum recommended by the United Nations. the Peacebuilding Fund reduced its funding for gender equality from 95.8 million to 49.9 million dollars between 2023 and 2024. Costa Rica urges that this gap be addressed through direct and sustained financing. Women's participation in political and peace processes reflects the same disparity. In 2024, women accounted for only 7% of negotiators and 14% of mediators in formal peace processes worldwide. This exclusion persists despite evidence demonstrating that peace agreements signed by women have higher rates of implementation and are more sustainable over time. We welcome the recognition in the Secretary-General's report on the future of peace operations that the full, equal and meaningful participation of women is essential to prevent a relapse into conflict and its call for gender parity in mission leadership. Mr President, women's inclusion must take place at every level of peacebuilding efforts, from local communities and grassroots organisations to the highest levels of decision-making within this organisation. For this reason, Costa Rica firmly reiterates its support for the candidacy of Rebecca Greenspan for Secretary-General of the United Nations, a Costa Rican woman, a daughter of peace, who has carried that conviction to places where peace is not an abstract concept but a daily necessity. Thank you.
I thank the representative of Costa Rica. I give the floor to the representative of Indonesia.

Thank you, Mr. President. Indonesia shares the view that women are not merely beneficiaries of peace, they are the architects of peace. Supporting women's leadership is therefore indispensable in preventing conflict and sustaining peace. Indonesia wishes to share two points. First, we must build on women's leadership at the grassroots. Indonesia has seen this firsthand. Women have helped communities recover from conflict, from supporting reconciliation after communal violence in central Sulawesi, to strengthening peace and resilience in Aceh following the Helsinki peace agreement. Indonesia's Desa Damai, or Peace Village, initiatives builds on this experience by empowering women to lead community dialogue and strengthen social cohesion. This reminds us that peace is built every day in villages, schools, and households. Our duty today is to recognize, strengthen, and institutionalize it. Yet globally, women's roles remain marginalized in peace processes. In 2024, women accounted for only 7% of negotiators and 14% of mediators worldwide, despite clear evidence that peace agreements involving women are more likely to be sustained. This brings me to my second point. Women's leadership must be mainstreamed at every level. Nationally, Indonesia integrates women's empowerment into our development priorities. including by bringing our national action plans on addressing social conflicts and preventing violent extremism closer to local communities. Regionally, Indonesia initiated the Southeast Asia Network of Women Peace Negotiators and Mediators. Internationally, more than 150 Indonesian women peacekeepers serve across UN peacekeeping missions. They build vital community trust and de-escalate local tensions. Indonesia also supports women contribution to national peace process, including in Afghanistan. Mr. President, the message is clear. When women participate fully, equally, and meaningfully, peace is more inclusive and more likely to endure. Therefore, Indonesia calls on member states to match today's discussions with political commitment, sustained resources, and strong institutional support for women's leadership, because a culture of peace cannot be sustained without women at its heart. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the representative of Indonesia. I give the floor to the representative of Ecuador.

Thank you, Mr. President. Ecuador has traditionally been a country of peace. Ecuadorians make up a nation that is accustomed to living in peace on a territory full of biodiversity, where four regions of extraordinary natural richness come together, the Amazon, the Andes, the coast and the Galapagos Islands, a country that extends across lush forests, snow-capped volcanoes and the coasts of the Pacific, a country that hosts one of the most unique ecosystems in the world. This tradition of peace has been threatened in recent years by new forms of violence that cross borders and which require coordinated responses. Transnational organized crime is today one of those threats. It has undermined the rule of law, institutions and peace, as well as development and democracy. The national government is addressing this scourge thinking about the future of young people and children. The magnitude of this challenge has shown us that building sustainable peace requires much more than just the absence of violence. It requires us to address the root causes of conflicts, strengthen institutions, promote social cohesion and build lasting solutions. In this context, the leadership of women is essential. A lot has been said about the disproportionate impact of violence upon women, but not enough has been said about their proven capacities as change makers, peace builders and protagonists in driving change in their communities. States must guarantee the full, equal, meaningful and safe participation of women in conflict prevention initiatives and peacekeeping processes, with the aim of achieving more resilient and inclusive societies and promoting a sustainable culture of peace. Mr President, achieving peace is a global responsibility. building a culture of peace is a lengthy complex and dynamic process which requires a spirit of mutual understanding and consultation Ecuador reiterates its commitment to the implementation of the program of action on a culture of peace and reaffirms the need for cooperation political dialogue and the peaceful settlement of disputes to prevail over confrontation violence and intolerance thank you very much
I thank the representative of Ecuador. I now give the floor to the representative of Mexico.

Thank you, Mr. President. Mexico welcomes the convening of this high-level forum and reaffirms its commitment to the program of action on a culture of peace. For Mexico, a culture of peace is built through dialogue, and the full participation of all people in the prevention and settlement of conflicts. And for this culture to be truly sustainable, women must be at the heart of those efforts as mediators, negotiators and peace builders. Women provide perspectives, knowledge and experiences that enrich the forging of consensus and which help to lay the groundwork for lasting peace. Therefore, their full, equal and meaningful participation must be seen at every level of action for peace. In accordance with our feminist foreign policy, Mexico has aimed to turn this conviction into concrete action. In that regard, I am pleased to announce that last week, Mexico presented its second national action plan on women, peace and security for the period 2026 to 2030 with a multi-level cross-cutting intersectional and intergenerational approach and with strengthened participation from civil society. This new roadmap builds upon the progress made since the adoption of our first plan of action in 2021. It also responds to new challenges from an increasingly complex security environment. It keeps the four pillars of the Women, Peace and Security agenda, prevention, participation, protection and relief and recovery, and it strengthens them with new priorities such as territorial peacebuilding. This same vision guides our work at the regional level. During our pro-temporary presidency of the Ibero-American Network of Women Mediators this year, Mexico strengthened its governance and institutions by connecting the experiences of women mediators and peacebuilders from the local level because peace doesn't just begin when a conflict ends. Peace begins when the voices of those making agreements are listened to and when they have a place at the table. And that is why Mexico reiterates that lasting peace requires the full, equal, and meaningful participation of women, and that is participation that is more than just symbolic and which takes the form of a true ability to have an impact and make decisions. Thank you very much.
I thank the representative of Mexico. I now give the floor to the representative of El Salvador.

Mr. President, El Salvador is grateful for the convening of this high-level forum and recognizes the importance of devoting this meeting to the leadership of women in promoting a culture of peace. Building a culture of peace requires us to address peace as a permanent process, which is strengthened much a long time before crises emerge and must be sustained after them. In these efforts, women's leadership is essential. For decades, women have contributed to sustaining communities, mediating tensions, supporting victims, preserving memory and rebuilding the fabric of society. However, that contribution is still not fully reflected in the spaces where decisions about peace and security are made. More than 25 years after the adoption of resolution 1325 of the Security Council, the Women, Peace and Security agenda provides us with a robust framework to close that gap, but normative progress has to be turned into concrete results. The participation in itself cannot be reduced just to being present, it has to mean a real ability to influence decisions, access resources, protection and recognition as actors for peace. President, as a member of the Peacebuilding Commission, El Salvador considers that the Commission has a particularly valuable role to play in bringing these perspectives to multilateral spaces, strengthening the participation of local peacebuilders and promoting greater consistency between prevention, peacebuilding and the Women, Peace and Security agenda. In this context, the support of the Peacebuilding Fund is particularly important. in El Salvador, the PBF's initiatives have helped strengthen women's organizations, expand institutional capacities, promote participation and leadership processes, support memory actions and psychosocial care, and generate intergenerational dialogue spaces focused on peacebuilding. This experience shows that investing in women's leadership is not just a way of achieving inclusion. It is an investment in prevention, social cohesion and the sustainability of peace. Our responsibility is to make sure that that leadership has space, the resources it needs and recognition. That's the only way we can move towards a culture of peace that is truly lasting and sustainable. Thank you very much.

I thank the representative of El Salvador. We have heard the last speaker for this meeting. Those delegations who were not able to deliver their statements are kindly requested to submit their statements to e-statements@un.org to be posted in the United Nations Journal. The High-level Forum on the Programme of Action on a Culture of Peace is now concluded. The meeting is adjourned.
